micros.title: Touch and Count: One Number per Object
micros.description: Counting a small group by touching each object exactly once while saying exactly one number name for it. Nothing gets skipped, nothing gets counted twice.
outcomes: Can touch-count up to 9 objects, one number name per object
Can slide counted objects into a 'done' pile so none are skipped or repeated

question.prompt: Count the stars: ⭐ ⭐ ⭐ ⭐. How many stars are there?

options.diagnosis: Skipped one star while counting.
Counted one star twice.
Recited the counting rhyme to the end instead of stopping at the last star.

question.explanation: Touch each star once as you count: 1, 2, 3, 4. There are 4 stars.

micros.title: The Last Number Tells How Many
micros.description: Understanding that after counting a group, the last number said is the size of the WHOLE group — you can answer 'how many?' without counting again.
outcomes: Can answer 'how many?' with the last number counted, without recounting
Can say how many objects are hiding after they are covered

question.prompt: Anu counts her bangles: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. How many bangles does she have in all?

options.text: She must count again to find out
options.diagnosis: Does not trust that the last number tells the size of the whole group.

options.text: Only the last bangle is called 6

options.diagnosis: Said the first number instead of the last.

question.explanation: The last number we say when counting tells how many there are altogether. Anu said 6 last, so she has 6 bangles.

micros.title: Still the Same Number: Count in Any Order
micros.description: Discovering that a group keeps its number when the objects are moved, spread out or counted in a different order. Rearranging changes how it looks, not how many.
outcomes: Can predict that a rearranged group still has the same count
Can count the same group starting from different objects and get the same answer

question.prompt: You counted 8 pebbles in a line. Then you push them all into one small heap. How many pebbles are in the heap?

options.diagnosis: Thinks squeezing the pebbles together makes fewer.

options.text: You cannot tell without counting again

question.explanation: No pebble came and no pebble went away, so there are still 8. Moving things around never changes how many there are.

micros.title: More, Fewer or the Same
micros.description: Comparing two small groups by matching objects one-to-one or by counting both, and saying which group has more, which has fewer, or that they are the same.
outcomes: Can match two groups object-to-object to see which has more
Can use the words more, fewer and same correctly for groups up to 9

micros.title: Reading and Writing 1 to 9
micros.description: Recognising the numerals 1 to 9, matching each numeral to a group of that many objects, and writing the numerals with correct strokes.
outcomes: Can point to the right numeral for a counted group
Can write the numerals 1 to 9 legibly
Can count out a requested number of objects from a bigger pile

micros.title: Zero Means None
micros.description: Meeting zero as the number for 'nothing there': an empty plate, an empty nest. Zero is a real number and a perfectly good answer to 'how many?'.
outcomes: Can answer 'how many?' with zero when a group is empty
Can say that zero means 'none' or 'nothing to count'

question.prompt: A nest had 2 birds. Both birds flew away. How many birds are in the nest now?

options.diagnosis: Answered with the starting amount instead of what is left.
Thinks at least one must always remain.

options.text: There is no number for an empty nest

question.explanation: Both birds are gone, so the nest has none. The number for 'none' is zero, written 0. Zero is a real number!

micros.title: Writing the Numeral 0
micros.description: Writing the symbol 0 and using it as an answer: whenever a count comes out empty, we write 0 just like any other number.
outcomes: Can write the numeral 0
Can write 0 as the answer when a group is empty

micros.title: Zero's Home: Just Before 1
micros.description: Placing zero in the number order — counting down 3, 2, 1, 0 and starting the number line at 0, just before 1.
outcomes: Can count down to zero (3, 2, 1, 0)
Can place 0 before 1 when ordering number cards

question.prompt: We count down: 2, 1, ___. What number comes next?

options.diagnosis: Counted up instead of down.
Placed zero after the other numbers, like on a phone keypad.

question.explanation: Counting down goes 2, 1, 0. Zero lives just before 1 — it is the number for 'none left'.

micros.title: Adding and Taking Away Zero
micros.description: Seeing with objects that adding zero or taking away zero changes nothing: 6 + 0 = 6 and 6 − 0 = 6. An empty plate joined to your plate adds no biscuits.
outcomes: Can answer n + 0 and n − 0 correctly for small numbers
Can explain with objects why adding zero changes nothing

question.prompt: What is 6 + 0?

options.diagnosis: Thinks adding zero destroys the number.
Treated the 0 as if it were 1 and counted on.
Wrote the two digits side by side instead of adding.

question.explanation: Adding 0 means adding nothing. You had 6, you added nothing, so you still have 6.

micros.title: Counting On Up to 20
micros.description: Saying the counting sequence from 1 to 20 without gaps and counting up to 20 objects accurately, with extra care on the tricky teen words.
outcomes: Can say the numbers 1 to 20 in order with no skips
Can count up to 20 objects accurately

question.prompt: Count on: 12, 13, 14, ___. What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Skipped fifteen in the teen sequence.
Repeated the last number instead of counting on.
Reversed the digits of fifteen.

question.explanation: The teen numbers go 13, 14, 15, 16, ... After 14 comes 15 — don't let fifteen hide!

micros.title: Teen Numbers: A Ten and Some More
micros.description: Building every teen number as one full group of ten plus loose ones — 14 is 10 and 4. Ten-frames and bundles make the hidden ten visible.
outcomes: Can show a teen number as one bundle of ten and loose ones
Can say how many tens and how many ones are in a teen number

question.prompt: One egg tray is full with 10 eggs, and 6 more eggs sit beside it. How many eggs in all?

options.diagnosis: Counted only the loose eggs; did not include the full tray of ten.
Wrote 10 and 6 side by side instead of combining them.
Reversed the tens and ones digits.

question.explanation: The tray is 10, then count on the loose eggs: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16. Ten and six make sixteen.

micros.title: Reading and Writing 10 to 20
micros.description: Reading and writing the numerals 10 to 20, writing the ten FIRST even though English says the ones first ('four-teen' is written 14, not 41).
outcomes: Can write the numeral for any spoken teen number
Can read 10 to 20 correctly without reversing digits

question.prompt: Which of these is the number fourteen?

options.diagnosis: Wrote the 'four' first because it is heard first.
Confused fourteen with forty.
Heard only the 'four' part of the word.

question.explanation: Fourteen is ten and four. We write the ten part first: 14. Careful — 41 is forty-one, a much bigger number!

micros.title: Before, After and Between up to 20
micros.description: Saying which number comes just before, just after or between given numbers up to 20, and arranging shuffled number cards in order starting from 0.
outcomes: Can say the number just before and just after any number up to 20
Can arrange number cards 0 to 20 in order

micros.title: Which Number Is More?
micros.description: Comparing two numbers up to 20 using counting order and ten-frames: the number that comes later in counting is more.
outcomes: Can say which of two numbers up to 20 is more and which is less
Can explain the answer using counting order or ten-frames

micros.title: Adding Is Putting Together
micros.description: Joining two small groups of objects and counting all of them to find the total. Meeting the plus sign and writing simple addition sentences like 3 + 2 = 5.
outcomes: Can join two groups of objects and count the total
Can write a matching addition sentence with + and =
Can act out simple joining stories

micros.title: Counting On from the Bigger Number
micros.description: Adding by putting the bigger number 'in your head' and counting on only the new jumps: for 9 + 4, say 9... then 10, 11, 12, 13. The start number is already done.
outcomes: Can add within 20 by counting on from the bigger number
Can show the jumps on fingers without counting the start number

question.prompt: What is 9 + 4?

options.diagnosis: Started counting at 9 instead of after it.
Counted one jump too many.
Subtracted instead of adding.

question.explanation: Put 9 in your head, then count on 4 jumps: 10, 11, 12, 13. So 9 + 4 = 13.

micros.title: Subtracting Is Taking Away
micros.description: Taking objects away from a group and counting what is left. Meeting the minus sign and discovering that order matters — you cannot take away more than you have.
outcomes: Can act out take-away stories and count what is left
Can write a matching subtraction sentence with − and =
Can explain why 4 − 9 cannot be acted out with real objects

question.prompt: Ravi has 4 laddoos on his plate. He wants to give 9 laddoos to his friend. What happens?

options.text: He cannot — he does not have 9 laddoos to give
He gives them, and 5 laddoos are left
options.diagnosis: Swapped the numbers and worked out 9 − 4 instead.
Added instead of taking away.

options.text: He gives them all and still has 4 left
options.diagnosis: Did not take anything away.

question.explanation: You can only take away what is there. Ravi has just 4 laddoos, so he cannot give 9. In take-away, the order of the numbers matters!

micros.title: Counting Back to Subtract
micros.description: Subtracting a small number by counting backwards from the start: for 11 − 2, say 11... then 10, 9. Count the jumps back, not the starting number.
outcomes: Can subtract within 20 by counting back
Can count the jumps back without counting the start number as a jump

question.prompt: What is 11 − 2?

options.diagnosis: Counted the starting number 11 as the first step back.
Added instead of subtracting.
Answered with the number being taken away.

question.explanation: Start at 11 and take 2 jumps back: 10, 9. So 11 − 2 = 9.

micros.title: The Make-a-Ten Trick
micros.description: Adding across ten by filling the ten first: for 8 + 5, give 2 to the 8 to make 10, then add the 3 that is left — 13. Ten-frames make the move visible.
outcomes: Can break the smaller number to make a ten and then add the rest
Can show the make-a-ten move on a ten-frame

micros.title: Missing Number Facts and the Balance Meaning of =
micros.description: Finding the missing number in facts like 5 + __ = 9, reading '=' as 'is the same as' — both sides of the equals sign must balance like a seesaw.
outcomes: Can find the missing number in facts like 9 + __ = 15
Can say whether number sentences like 6 + 1 = 5 + 2 are true or false

question.prompt: Find the missing number: 5 + ___ = 9

options.diagnosis: Added the two numbers seen instead of making both sides the same.
Stopped counting up one number too early.
Repeated the total instead of finding the missing part.

question.explanation: Both sides of = must be the same amount. Count up from 5 to 9: 6, 7, 8, 9 — that is 4 jumps. So 5 + 4 = 9.

micros.title: Making Bundles of Ten
micros.description: Grouping loose sticks into bundles of ten and counting bundles by tens: 3 bundles means 10, 20, 30. Groups of ten are the building blocks of big numbers.
outcomes: Can bundle loose objects into groups of ten
Can count bundles by tens: 10, 20, 30, ...

micros.title: Tens and Ones Inside a Number
micros.description: Seeing that a 2-digit number is made of tens and ones: 47 is 4 bundles of ten (forty) and 7 loose ones. The place of a digit tells what it is worth.
outcomes: Can say how many tens and ones are in any 2-digit number
Can build a given 2-digit number from bundles and loose sticks

question.prompt: In the number 53, what does the digit 5 stand for?

options.diagnosis: Applied 'ones' to the tens place.
Thinks each digit stands for the whole number.

question.explanation: In 53 the 5 sits in the tens place, so it means 5 tens = 50. The 3 means 3 ones. Together: 50 + 3 = 53.

micros.title: Reading and Writing 2-digit Numbers
micros.description: Writing 2-digit numbers from their names using place-value cards: 'sixty-three' is the 60 card with the 3 sliding over the 0 — two digits, 63, never 603.
outcomes: Can write the numeral for a spoken 2-digit number
Can read any 2-digit number aloud correctly

question.prompt: How do we write the number sixty-three?

options.diagnosis: Wrote 'sixty' then 'three' side by side.
Reversed the tens and ones digits.
Wrote the sixty but dropped the three ones.

question.explanation: Sixty-three is 6 tens and 3 ones. The 3 sits in the ones place of 60, so we write 63 — just two digits.

micros.title: Counting Past 39, 49, 59...
micros.description: Counting smoothly across decade numbers: after 49 the ten ones bundle into a new ten, making 50. The 100-chart shows the same jump at the end of every row.
outcomes: Can count on across any decade (39 to 40, 59 to 60) without stalling
Can explain with bundles why 49 + 1 makes 50

question.prompt: Count on: 48, 49, ___. What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Jumped to the wrong decade after 49.
Went backwards to the start of the decade.

question.explanation: After 49, the ten loose ones make a new bundle: 4 tens and 10 ones become 5 tens. The next number is 50.

micros.title: Skip Counting by Tens
micros.description: Counting by tens from 10 to 90 — forwards and backwards — and noticing that the ones digit stays 0 while the tens digit climbs.
outcomes: Can skip count by tens: 10, 20, 30, ... 90
Can continue a tens count from any decade number

micros.title: Naming Coins and Notes
micros.description: Recognising and naming the common coins (₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10) and notes (₹10, ₹20, ₹50) by reading the value printed on each one.
outcomes: Can name the common coins and notes
Can find and read the printed value on any coin or note

micros.title: Which Is Worth More?
micros.description: Comparing coins and notes by the printed number, not by size or shininess. A small ₹2 coin beats a big old ₹1 coin.
outcomes: Can compare two coins or notes by their printed values
Can explain that a coin's size does not decide its value

question.prompt: An old ₹1 coin is big. A new ₹2 coin is small. Which coin is worth more?

options.text: The ₹2 coin — the printed number 2 is more than 1
The ₹1 coin, because it is bigger
They are worth the same — one coin each
options.diagnosis: Counted pieces of money instead of reading the values.
Judges value by how the coin feels, not by the printed number.

question.explanation: The number printed on a coin tells its value. 2 is more than 1, so the small ₹2 coin is worth more than the big ₹1 coin.

micros.title: Adding Up Coins and Notes
micros.description: Finding the total of two or three small coins and notes by counting on from the biggest value: a ₹10 note and a ₹2 coin make 10... 11, 12.
outcomes: Can find the total of two or three coins and notes
Can count on by each piece's value, not by pieces

question.prompt: Meena has a ₹5 coin, a ₹2 coin and a ₹1 coin. How much money does she have?

options.diagnosis: Counted 3 pieces of money instead of adding the values.
Missed adding one of the coins.
Wrote the values side by side instead of adding them.

question.explanation: Add the printed values: 5, then 2 more makes 7, then 1 more makes 8. Meena has ₹8.

micros.title: Same Money, Different Coins
micros.description: Showing one amount in different ways — two ₹5 coins are worth the same as one ₹10 coin. Fewer pieces can still be more money.
outcomes: Can show a small amount using different sets of coins
Can check whether two sets of coins are worth the same by adding values

question.prompt: Which of these is worth the SAME as one ₹10 note?

options.diagnosis: Seven coins feel like a lot, but they total only ₹7.
Did not add the values — three ₹2 coins make only ₹6.
Picked the biggest single coin without checking; ₹5 is only half of ₹10.

question.explanation: Five ₹2 coins make 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10, the same as the ₹10 note. The other choices total ₹7, ₹6 and ₹5.

micros.title: Circle, Triangle, Square, Rectangle
micros.description: Naming the four basic flat shapes and telling them apart by counting sides and corners: a triangle has 3, a square and rectangle have 4, a circle has none.
outcomes: Can name circle, triangle, square and rectangle
Can count the sides and corners of a flat shape

question.prompt: How many corners does a square have?

options.diagnosis: Confused the square with a triangle.
Confused the square with a circle.

options.text: It depends on how the square sits
options.diagnosis: Thinks turning a shape changes what it is.

question.explanation: Every square has 4 straight sides and 4 corners, however it sits. Counting sides and corners is how we know a shape's name.

micros.title: Still the Same Shape: Any Size, Any Turn
micros.description: Recognising shapes even when they are turned, tilted, skinny or huge. A tilted square is still a square; a long thin triangle is still a triangle — check the sides and corners, not the pose.
outcomes: Can recognise a square, triangle or rectangle in any turn or size
Can decide 'triangle or not' by counting 3 straight sides and 3 corners

question.prompt: A shape is very long and thin. It has 3 straight sides and 3 corners. What is it?

options.text: Not a real triangle — it is too thin

options.diagnosis: Did not count — a rectangle has 4 sides, this shape has 3.
Judged by the look instead of counting sides and corners.

question.explanation: Any shape with 3 straight sides and 3 corners is a triangle — thin, fat, upside-down or tilted. The count decides, not the look!

micros.title: Roll, Slide or Stack?
micros.description: Exploring solid objects with hands: round things like balls roll, flat-faced things like boxes slide and stack, and a can does both. Sorting solids by what they can do.
outcomes: Can sort everyday solids by whether they roll, slide or stack
Can explain that round parts roll and flat parts slide or stack

micros.title: Flat Shapes and Solid Objects
micros.description: Telling a flat (2D) shape from a solid (3D) object: a ball is a solid, not a 'circle' — the circle is what you see when you trace or stamp a solid's face on paper.
outcomes: Can tell whether something is a flat shape or a solid object
Can predict what flat shape a solid's face will print or trace

question.prompt: Amit dips the flat end of a round can in paint and stamps it on paper. What shape does it print?

options.diagnosis: Gave the solid's name instead of its flat face's shape.
Did not picture the round end of the can.
Mixed up solids and the flat shapes on their faces.

question.explanation: The can is a solid, but its flat end is a circle. Stamping prints that flat face — a circle — on the paper.

micros.title: Shape Hunt: Shapes Hiding Around Us
micros.description: Finding shapes in everyday things on a shape hunt — a roti is round like a circle, a door is a rectangle, a samosa face is a triangle — and saying which shape is seen.
outcomes: Can find and name shapes in everyday objects
Can collect and share examples of each shape from home or class

micros.title: The Right Comparing Words
micros.description: Using the precise words of comparing: longer/shorter, taller/shorter, heavier/lighter, holds more/holds less — instead of saying 'big' for everything.
outcomes: Can pick the right comparing word for a situation
Can say the opposite of each comparing word

micros.title: Fair Length Tests: Same Starting Line
micros.description: Comparing two lengths fairly by putting both objects' starting ends on the same line before looking at which reaches farther. Catching the trick when one object is pushed ahead.
outcomes: Can line up two objects from the same end before comparing
Can spot an unfair comparison where the starting ends are offset

question.prompt: Two pencils lie on the table. The red pencil is pushed ahead, so its tip sticks out farther. Is the red pencil longer?

options.text: We can't tell yet — first line up both starting ends
Yes — its tip sticks out farther
Yes — the fatter pencil is always longer
options.diagnosis: Mixed up thick with long.

options.text: No — the blue one is longer
options.diagnosis: Guessed the opposite without doing a fair test.

question.explanation: Sticking out farther only counts if both pencils start from the same line. Line up the ends first, then see which reaches farther.

micros.title: Shortest to Longest
micros.description: Ordering three objects by length from shortest to longest using the same-starting-line rule, and using words like 'the longest' and 'the shortest'.
outcomes: Can order three objects from shortest to longest
Can point out the longest and the shortest of three objects

micros.title: Heavier or Lighter?
micros.description: Comparing weights by holding one object in each hand or using a simple pan balance — and discovering that bigger does NOT always mean heavier.
outcomes: Can guess and then check which of two objects is heavier
Can give an example where the smaller object is heavier

question.prompt: A big soft pillow and a small iron lock — which is heavier?

options.text: The pillow, because it is so big and puffy
options.diagnosis: Judges weight by size and puffiness.
Guessed equality instead of comparing in two hands.

question.explanation: Bigger does not mean heavier! The pillow is full of soft, light stuffing, but the little lock is solid iron. Hold one in each hand to feel it.

micros.title: Which Holds More?
micros.description: Comparing how much two containers hold by pouring with a small cup and counting cupfuls. A tall thin bottle can hold less than a short wide pot — pouring tells the truth.
outcomes: Can compare two containers by pouring and counting cupfuls
Can explain that taller does not always mean holds more

question.prompt: A tall thin bottle and a short wide pot. How can we find out which holds more water?

options.text: Fill each with cupfuls of water and count the cups
The tall bottle holds more — tall things always hold more
The bigger-looking one holds more, no need to check
options.diagnosis: Uses 'big' for everything instead of testing.
Chose a test that does not measure how much they hold.

question.explanation: Pour and count! If the pot takes 6 cups and the bottle takes 4, the pot holds more — even though the bottle is taller.

micros.title: Day and Night
micros.description: Telling day from night by looking at the sky — sun means day, moon and stars mean night — not by what we happen to be doing. A nap in the afternoon still happens in the day.
outcomes: Can tell whether it is day or night from the sky
Can name things that happen in the day and at night

question.prompt: Riya takes a nap after lunch while the sun is shining outside. Is it day or night?

options.text: Night — because her curtains are closed
options.diagnosis: Thinks a dark room makes it night.

options.text: It is no time at all
options.diagnosis: Does not connect the moment to day or night.

question.explanation: Day and night depend on the sky, not on what we are doing. The sun is up, so it is day — even if Riya is asleep!

micros.title: Morning, Afternoon, Evening, Night
micros.description: Naming the four parts of the day in order and matching everyday activities to them: breakfast in the morning, play in the evening, sleep at night.
outcomes: Can say the parts of the day in order
Can match common activities to the right part of the day

micros.title: First, Next, Last: Before and After
micros.description: Putting 3-4 daily events in order and using before, after, yesterday, today and tomorrow correctly, anchored to real remembered events.
outcomes: Can put 3-4 picture cards of daily events in the right order
Can use before/after and yesterday/today/tomorrow correctly

question.prompt: First Anu pours milk into her glass. Then she drinks it. Which happens AFTER the pouring?

options.diagnosis: Swapped before and after.

options.text: Both happen at the same time
options.diagnosis: Does not yet see the two events as a sequence.
Cannot order two events even when the story gives the order.

question.explanation: First pour, then drink — you cannot drink milk that is not in the glass yet! Drinking comes after pouring.

micros.title: Which Takes Longer?
micros.description: Comparing how long two activities take using a fair measure — claps, steps or a sand timer — because boring things only FEEL long. Feelings are not clocks.
outcomes: Can say which of two activities takes longer
Can time short activities by counting claps or using a sand timer

question.prompt: Which takes LONGER: washing your hands, or a whole day at school?

options.diagnosis: Washing feels long because it is boring, but feelings are not clocks.
Compared without thinking about the real durations.
Does not yet see that any two durations can be compared.

question.explanation: A school day lasts many hours; washing hands takes less time than one song. We compare how long things really take, not how they feel.

micros.title: Copy It, Continue It
micros.description: Copying a simple repeating pattern (red-blue, red-blue) with beads, claps or drawings, and continuing it correctly by following the repeat — not by copying the last item.
outcomes: Can copy a simple AB pattern of colours, shapes, sounds or actions
Can say and place what comes next in an AB pattern

question.prompt: The fruit line goes: banana, apple, banana, apple, banana, ___. What comes next?

options.diagnosis: Repeated the last fruit seen instead of following the repeat.
Added any fruit — treats the pattern as decoration without a rule.
Doubled an element instead of following the banana-apple unit.

question.explanation: The chunk 'banana-apple' repeats. After banana always comes apple. So the next fruit is an apple.

micros.title: Find the Chunk That Repeats
micros.description: Circling the whole unit that repeats in a pattern — including trickier units like clap-stomp-stomp, where the doubled element must be counted twice.
outcomes: Can point out or circle the repeating unit of a pattern
Can extend ABB and AAB patterns one whole unit at a time

question.prompt: The pattern goes: sun, sun, moon, sun, sun, moon. Which chunk keeps repeating?

options.diagnosis: Counted the doubled sun only once.
Ignored the moon; picked only part of the unit.
Picked the most noticeable item instead of the whole unit.

question.explanation: The whole chunk 'sun-sun-moon' comes again and again. The unit is the WHOLE group that repeats — both suns and the moon.

micros.title: Pattern or Not?
micros.description: Telling a true pattern from a random arrangement with one test: can you say for sure what comes next? If yes, it is a pattern; if not, it is just decoration.
outcomes: Can decide whether an arrangement is a pattern or random
Can use the 'what comes next?' test and explain the answer

question.prompt: A string of beads goes: red, green, yellow, blue, red, purple. Is it a pattern?

options.text: No — no chunk repeats, so we cannot say what comes next

options.diagnosis: One repeated colour is not a repeating unit.

options.text: Yes — every string of beads is a pattern

question.explanation: In a real pattern a chunk repeats, so you always know what comes next. Here the colours come in no order — pretty, but not a pattern.

micros.title: Make Your Own Pattern
micros.description: Creating an own repeating pattern with beads, stamps, sounds or body moves, saying its rule aloud, and challenging a friend to continue it.
outcomes: Can create a repeating pattern and say its unit aloud
Can check whether a friend continued the pattern correctly

micros.title: Sort by One Rule
micros.description: Sorting objects into groups by one spoken rule (colour, shape, size or use) and sticking to that rule for every single object — no switching midway.
outcomes: Can sort a set of objects by a given rule
Can check each object against the rule card before placing it

question.prompt: We are sorting toys by COLOUR. The red pile has a red ball, a red block and a red car. Where does a BLUE car go?

options.text: Not in the red pile — it goes with the blue things
In the red pile, because it is a car like the red car
In the red pile, because it is a nice car
options.diagnosis: Groups by liking instead of the rule.

options.text: In whichever pile has more space
options.diagnosis: Places objects without checking the rule at all.

question.explanation: Our rule is colour, so we ask only one question: is it red? The blue car is not red, so it cannot join the red pile — even though it is a car.

micros.title: Guess My Rule
micros.description: Looking at an already-sorted group and working out the rule: asking 'what is the SAME about everything in this pile?' — a shared attribute, not a story or a favourite.
outcomes: Can state the rule used to sort a given group
Can say what is the same about all objects in a pile

question.prompt: One pile has: a banana, a lemon, a sunflower and a yellow ball. What is the sorting rule?

options.diagnosis: Checked only some objects — a sunflower and a ball are not fruits.
Made up a story instead of finding what is the same.
Did not check every object — a banana is not round.

question.explanation: A sorting rule must be true for EVERY object in the pile. The only thing all four share is the colour yellow.

micros.title: Every Object Gets a Home
micros.description: Finishing a sort completely: a good rule splits ALL the objects, so nothing is left over. Using an 'others' or 'not-red' group for things that don't fit the first pile.
outcomes: Can sort every object, using a 'not-...' group when needed
Can re-sort the same objects with a different rule

question.prompt: We are sorting toys into two groups: RED and NOT RED. Where does a green spinning top go?

options.text: Nowhere — it does not belong anywhere

options.diagnosis: Placed it without checking the colour rule.

options.text: We keep it aside, outside the sorting
options.diagnosis: Leaves objects out instead of using the not-red home.

question.explanation: The top is green, so it is not red — and 'not red' is a real home! A good sort finds a place for every single object.

micros.title: Count the Groups: More or Fewer?
micros.description: After sorting, counting how many objects landed in each group and saying which group has more, which has fewer — our very first step of reading data.
outcomes: Can count the objects in each sorted group
Can say which group has more and which has fewer
